title: Nilesh Shah Bets on Earnings Recovery in Samvat 2083, Picks Three Sectors
excerpt: Kotak Mahindra AMC's managing director expects FY27 earnings growth of 12-15% for large-caps and flags banking, premium consumption and modern manufacturing as the Samvat 2083 opportunities.
body:
• Kotak Mahindra AMC managing director Nilesh Shah expects an earnings-led recovery in Samvat 2083, forecasting FY27 earnings growth of 12-15% for large-caps, 20-25% for mid-caps and 15-20% for small-caps.
  • His three sectors to watch are banking and financial services, premium consumption and modern manufacturing.
  • Shah says investors are effectively buying India nearly 30% cheaper than at the peak valuations of two years ago, but warns against expecting 30% annual returns.
  • For investors, the practical takeaway is that returns this Samvat will come from earnings delivery, not a valuation rerating — Shah's own advice stresses SIPs and asset allocation over market timing.

As Samvat 2083 begins, Kotak Mahindra AMC managing director Nilesh Shah is betting on an earnings recovery to drive Indian equities, rather than another round of valuation expansion. Speaking after a North America roadshow that took in sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, endowments and family offices, Shah told The Hindu BusinessLine that global investors remain actively engaged with India, with several institutions already committing capital and others evaluating allocations. "Not a single investor said they did not want to meet," he said.

The earnings numbers behind the call

Shah expects FY27 earnings growth of 12-15% for large-caps, 20-25% for mid-caps and 15-20% for small-caps. That, in his telling, is where returns will come from. In a separate interview with Value Research, he described his stance as cautiously optimistic and said investors should expect moderate, earnings-led returns rather than a rerating boom, with volatility persisting through the year. Brokerage forecasts compiled for the new Samvat point the same way: FY27 Nifty earnings growth estimates range from 13.4% at SBI Securities to 18% at Kotak Neo, after a Samvat 2082 in which the Sensex fell 7.9% and the Nifty 50 dropped 6.8% through November 4.

"India is a structural bull market available at a cyclical valuation discount."

— Nilesh Shah, Managing Director, Kotak Mahindra AMC

The three sectors

First, banking and financial services. Shah believes banks are entering one of their strongest phases, backed by healthy credit growth, low non-performing assets and strong balance sheets. Second, premium consumption. He expects the upcoming 8th Pay Commission to lift discretionary spending across automobiles, travel, consumer durables and hospitality, favouring companies selling to affluent consumers. Third, modern manufacturing, where he sees Indian firms continuing to deepen their role in global supply chains. The three picks share a common thread: each depends on domestic demand or on earnings that do not need foreign flows to materialise.

Valuations, and what not to expect

Shah argues that the correction has reset expectations. Compared with where valuations stood two years ago, he said, investors are effectively buying India nearly 30% cheaper today. But he was explicit about the ceiling on that opportunity: "If you're expecting 30 per cent annual returns, India is not the market for you. But if you're looking for high-single-digit to low-double-digit compounding over a decade, India remains one of the best investment opportunities globally." He also noted that the current rally is being driven largely by underweight investors moving back to benchmark allocations, rather than a broad "overweight India" trade — a distinction that caps how far momentum alone can run.

Triggers and a tax argument

Looking ahead, Shah pointed to four triggers: implementation of the 8th Pay Commission, a turnaround in foreign portfolio inflows as investors rotate out of crowded AI trades and back into emerging markets, healthy corporate earnings growth, and tax-policy reform. On taxes, he argued that the coexistence of the Securities Transaction Tax (STT) and long-term capital gains tax creates distortions: "STT was introduced in lieu of capital gains tax. From an investor's perspective, one of them should go." He also said that while India can sustain 5-7% growth, sustained double-digit expansion will require reforms in land, labour, ease of doing business and project execution.

What it means for diaspora investors

For NRI investors adding to India allocations around Diwali and the November 8 Muhurat session, Shah's message is a discipline check rather than a shopping list: the Samvat 2083 case rests on companies delivering double-digit earnings growth at valuations well below their peak, not on multiples expanding again. His FY27 growth ladder — strongest in mid-caps — also explains why he pairs the sector call with a warning to favour systematic investing and asset allocation over trying to time the recovery.
